The initial phases of NLR’s research surveyed early initiatives of AV technology demonstration, with Phase I research documenting 10 early deployment sites in the first edition of The Automated Mobility District Implementation Catalog (Young and Lott 2020). The 10 sites spanned settings that included urban districts, sports complexes, university campuses, and master-planned residential communities. When published in 2020, it compiled lessons learned from the initial phase of demonstration pilot projects, primarily from the view of the sponsoring public agencies, with further insight included from the perspectives of the operating companies and AV technology developers. The first edition is available at docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy20osti/76551.pdf. Subsequently, Phase II research collected and evaluated the lessons learned from these early deployment sites, with particular attention to fleet operations, impacts of service reliability, and vehicle technology evolution as the field of companies was being progressively winnowed by the challenges of full automation. The Phase II research findings were documented in the second edition of The Automated Mobility District Implementation Catalog (Young and Lott 2022). The second edition used a framework of “cardinal principles” gleaned primarily from common observations and assessments of the 10 early deployment sites for the safe and efficient application of AV technology in managed fleet deployments and the projection of those principles to future AMDs at scale. The second edition is available at docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy22osti/83276.pdf. Both Phase I and Phase II emphasized the context of AV technology deployment and passenger transport services within a dense urban setting and other major activity centers with intense passenger origin-destination demand patterns, such as those found in large business districts, airports, and university and medical campuses. This third edition of the report series provides an overview of the most significant findings of Phase I and Phase II research as well as an overview of the Phase III research findings. This report also contains an update on the 10 early AV deployment sites that have been tracked throughout the automated mobility district (AMD) implementation research to this point. As such, this report is intended to be a stand-alone summary of all three phases. The full details of the Phase III research will be published as subsequent editions in the report series. The Phase III research has examined battery electric vehicles (BEVs) operating in a fully automated fleet within an AMD setting—typically with multiple fleets providing different types 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. of mobility services, many of which are dispatched on demand as the vehicle fleet operations dynamically respond to rider requests. Drawing from this focused examination, Phase III studies have further assessed the implications of the simultaneous transformations of automation, electrification, and on-demand services for AVs operating as a “multimodal” transportation system within a large AMD. Topics investigated have included the comparisons and contrasts between traditional fixed-route transit services with those of on-demand transit (ODT) services.
